subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The SI unit of the Young modulus is the same as that of:
questions.explain: Strain is dimensionless, so the Young modulus has the units of stress, the pascal.

questions.q: When a wire is loaded only up to its limit of proportionality and then unloaded, the loading and unloading lines on a force–extension graph:
questions.explain: Within the elastic (proportional) region, loading and unloading follow the same straight line.

questions.q: A spring extends 0.040 m when a force of 8.0 N is applied. Its spring constant is:
The elastic limit of a material is the point beyond which:
options: The material no longer returns to its original length when unloaded
questions.explain: Beyond the elastic limit, deformation becomes permanent (plastic).

questions.q: Hooke's law states that, up to the limit of proportionality:
options: Force is inversely proportional to extension
Extension is proportional to the applied force
questions.explain: Hooke's law: extension is directly proportional to the applied force, F = kx.

questions.q: A force–extension graph for a metal wire shows a straight line then curves over before fracture. The straight portion corresponds to:
questions.explain: The initial straight-line region is the elastic region where Hooke's law holds.

questions.q: A steel wire and a rubber band are both stretched. Compared with steel, rubber typically has a:
questions.explain: Rubber is far more easily stretched than steel, so it has a much lower Young modulus.

questions.q: Density is defined as:
questions.explain: Density ρ = mass ÷ volume, with units kg m⁻³.

questions.q: Two wires of the same material but different lengths and areas are tested. The Young modulus is:
options: The same for both, since it is a property of the material
questions.explain: The Young modulus is an intrinsic material property, independent of the specimen's dimensions.

questions.q: The spring constant k represents:
options: The stiffness — force needed per unit extension
questions.explain: k is the stiffness, the force required to produce unit extension (N m⁻¹).

questions.q: The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched material equals:
options: The area under the force–extension graph
The gradient of the force–extension graph
questions.explain: Work done in stretching, and hence energy stored, equals the area under the force–extension graph.

questions.q: A wire under a stress of 1.5 × 10⁸ Pa has a strain of 7.5 × 10⁻⁴. Its Young modulus is:
Breaking stress is best described as:
options: The maximum stress a material can withstand before it fractures
The stress at the limit of proportionality
questions.explain: Breaking (ultimate tensile) stress is the maximum stress a material can bear before breaking.

questions.q: Tensile strain is defined as:
questions.explain: Strain ε = extension ÷ original length and is a dimensionless ratio.

questions.q: The Young modulus of a material is defined as:
questions.explain: The Young modulus E = tensile stress ÷ tensile strain.

questions.q: The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched spring (obeying Hooke's law) is given by:
questions.explain: Energy stored = area under the force–extension line = ½Fx = ½kx².

questions.q: On a stress–strain graph, the Young modulus is given by:
options: The gradient of the initial linear (straight-line) region
questions.explain: E equals the gradient of the linear (Hooke's-law) part of the stress–strain graph.

questions.q: A wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries a tension of 40 N. The tensile stress is:
On a stress–strain graph, a material that absorbs a large amount of energy (large area under the curve) before fracture is described as:
questions.explain: A large area under the stress–strain curve means much energy absorbed before fracture, i.e. the material is tough.

questions.q: A brittle material is one that:
options: Undergoes large plastic deformation before breaking
Breaks suddenly with little or no plastic deformation
questions.explain: Brittle materials (e.g. glass) fracture abruptly with negligible plastic deformation.

questions.q: A material is described as 'stiff' if it has a:
questions.explain: Stiffness corresponds to a high Young modulus: large stress produces only small strain.

questions.q: The limit of proportionality on a force–extension graph is the point beyond which:
options: Force is no longer proportional to extension
questions.explain: Beyond the limit of proportionality, extension is no longer directly proportional to force (Hooke's law fails).

questions.q: On a force–extension graph for a spring obeying Hooke's law, the gradient equals:
questions.explain: The gradient of a force–extension graph is the spring constant k.

questions.q: A spring of constant 50 N m⁻¹ is extended by 0.20 m. The elastic strain energy stored is:
Tensile stress is defined as:
questions.explain: Stress σ = force ÷ cross-sectional area, with units Pa (N m⁻²).

questions.q: Elastic deformation means that when the load is removed, the material:
questions.explain: Elastic deformation is fully recoverable: the material returns to its original shape.

questions.q: A ductile material is one that:
options: Can undergo large plastic deformation and be drawn into wires
Does not obey Hooke's law at all
questions.explain: Ductile materials (e.g. copper) deform plastically a great deal and can be drawn into wires.

questions.q: Plastic deformation is characterised by:
options: A permanent change in shape after the load is removed
questions.explain: Plastic deformation leaves a permanent extension once the load is removed.

questions.q: An object of mass 240 g has a volume of 30 cm³. Its density is:
The yield point of a ductile material marks where:
options: The material begins to extend rapidly with little extra force (plastic flow)
The wire returns to its original length
questions.explain: At the yield point the material yields, undergoing large plastic extension for little additional stress.
